segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was on his way and nearing Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and falling to the ground he heard a voice saying to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who are you, Lord?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he replied,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The men traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Saul got up from the ground, but though his eyes were open he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For three days he was without sight, and he neither ate nor drank.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Ananias.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Here I am, Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Lord said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get up and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man from Tarsus named Saul; for look, he is praying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he may see again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Ananias answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much harm he has done to your holy ones in Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Lord said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go, for this man is my chosen instrument to carry my name before Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For I myself will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Ananias went and entered the house. Laying his hands on him, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brother Saul, the Lord has sent me, Jesus who appeared to you on the road as you were coming, so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once something like scales fell from his eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after taking food he regained his strength. He spent some days with the disciples in Damascus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once he began proclaiming in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who heard him were astonished and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Isn’t this the man who wreaked havoc in Jerusalem on those who call on this name? And hadn’t he come here for this very purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Saul grew all the more powerful and confounded the Jews living in Damascus, proving that this man is the Messiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted together to kill him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but their plot became known to Saul. They were even watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles, and described to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, and that the Lord had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he was with them, going in and out in Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He spoke and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they were trying to kill him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the brothers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the assembly throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up; and walking in the fear of the Lord and in the encouragement of the Holy Spirit, it grew in number.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now as Peter was traveling through all those parts, he came down also to the holy ones living in Lydda.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There he found a man named Aeneas, who had been lying on a mat for eight years, for he was paralyzed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once he got up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now in Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, which translated is Dorcas. She was full of good works and of the acts of charity that she did.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days she became ill and died. They washed her and laid her in an upstairs room.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him with the plea,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not delay in coming to us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him up to the upstairs room, and all the widows stood beside him, weeping and showing the tunics and cloaks that Dorcas had made while she was with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter sent them all outside, knelt down, and prayed. Then, turning to the body, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tabitha, get up.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He gave her his hand and raised her up; then, calling the holy ones and the widows, he presented her alive.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he stayed in Joppa for many days with a certain Simon, a tanner.

notes.note: In Acts ‘the Way’ is a name the early followers of Jesus used for their own movement. The Greek word is the ordinary one for a road or journey, and it is the same word translated ‘road’ in verses 17 and 27, so Saul meets Jesus on the road while hunting people of the Way.

The Greek address can be a respectful ‘sir’ or the title ‘Lord’. Saul does not yet know who is speaking, but he is answering a voice from heaven, so the stronger sense is kept here, as in most translations. Some interpreters prefer ‘sir’ at this point.

The Greek word means both ‘voice’ and ‘sound’. In Paul’s own retelling at Acts 22:9 his companions ‘did not hear the voice’ of the one speaking, and many interpreters reconcile the two by taking this verse to mean that they heard a sound without making out words. Whether the grammar itself signals that distinction is disputed.

The traditional rendering is ‘saints’, which many translations keep. The word is used here of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other translations use ‘God’s people’ or ‘his holy people’.

The Greek word means ‘peoples’ or ‘nations’, and in the plural it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the one Greek word as ‘Gentiles’ or ‘nations’ according to sense. Here the contrast with ‘the children of Israel’ makes ‘Gentiles’ the natural choice.

The traditional rendering is ‘the Christ’. Here the word is a title under debate in the synagogues, the anointed king Israel expected, and ‘Messiah’ conveys that to a modern reader. Where the word functions as part of Jesus’s name, as in verse 34, ‘Christ’ is kept. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

The earliest manuscripts read ‘his disciples’, meaning people Saul had won over in Damascus. Many later manuscripts read ‘the disciples took him’, which avoids the surprise of Saul already having disciples of his own. Paul mentions the same escape in 2 Corinthians 11:32–33.

The traditional rendering is ‘Hellenists’ (older versions, ‘Grecians’). The word is rare, and most scholars take it here to mean Jews whose language was Greek, many of them from the diaspora, as distinct from Aramaic-speaking Jews. This is the circle Stephen had argued with in Acts 6. ‘Hellenists’ leaves a modern reader guessing, so the sense is spelled out.

The traditional rendering is ‘church’, which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled, whereas ‘church’ now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses ‘assembly’ throughout so that the one Greek word stays visible. It refers here to the whole community across three regions, not a single meeting.

The Greek says only ‘spread for yourself’, with no object. Most take it to mean spreading his own bedding, something a paralyzed man could not do. The same verb is used of preparing a dining couch, so ‘get yourself something to eat’ is also possible.
Tabitha is Aramaic and Dorcas is Greek; both mean ‘gazelle’. Luke gives his Greek-speaking readers the equivalent name, and she was probably known by both in a mixed port town like Joppa.

Tanners worked with animal carcasses and foul-smelling materials, and later Jewish sources treat the trade as disreputable and its practitioners as kept at a distance. Many interpreters think Luke mentions Peter’s host deliberately, as a prelude to the next chapter’s vision about what is clean and unclean. Luke himself does not say so.

candidates.reason: Used across the New Testament for community members of both sexes; translations split between ‘brothers’, ‘brothers and sisters’ and ‘believers’, and the choice should be uniform.
Occurs in Acts 6:1, 9:29 and (variant) 11:20; ‘Hellenists’ is opaque, and the rendering should match across those passages.
Translations vary between ‘comfort’, ‘encouragement’, ‘consolation’ and ‘exhortation’ across Luke–Acts, Paul and Hebrews; the word and its verb need a governed set of renderings by sense.
The traditional ‘alms’ is archaic; it recurs in Matthew 6, Luke and Acts, and needs one modern equivalent.
The poor person’s pallet appears in Mark, John and Acts and is rendered ‘bed’, ‘mat’, ‘pallet’ or ‘cot’; readers should see one word.

warnings: Verse 26: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
